query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Engineering a nanohierarchical architecture with spatial composition undulation into the high‐entropy alloy will promote the in‐situ formation of an adaptive friction interface, thereby reducing both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service‐temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional high‐entropy alloy with a relatively homogeneous microstructure lacking engineered nanoprecipitates or nano‐coupled grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled composition variations and rapid solidification processing (or equivalent advanced processing) to generate a nanohierarchical architecture that includes nano‐coupled grains and nanoprecipitates.
generation.conditions: Under sliding conditions typical of self‐lubricating moving components and across a broad temperature range (from room temperature up to about 800 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoprecipitate-rich regions and nano‐coupled grain structures that, under operational stress, evolve into a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: The integrated nanostructure relieves gradient frictional stresses via the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways at lower temperatures while activating an in‐situ formed, lubricious glaze layer at high temperatures. This adaptive friction interface minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear in addition to reducing friction by offering a continuously renewed low‐shear interface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the treated alloy is predicted to exhibit a markedly lower coefficient of friction and a reduced wear rate (potentially by an order of magnitude reduction in wear rate, while the precise friction reduction is uncertain) under identical sliding conditions and thermal environments.
generation.baseline: The untreated high‐entropy alloy which, under dynamic sliding conditions, exhibits higher friction coefficients and wear rates over the same temperature range.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected to be limited if the processing parameters do not achieve the desired nanostructural modulation or if operating temperatures exceed approximately 800 °C, where phase stability and the integrity of the glaze layer might be compromised.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in friction and wear reduction remain uncertain due to potential variability in the microstructural evolution, and long-term stability under cyclic operating conditions has not been fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one group processed to induce the nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation, and a control group with a conventional homogeneous microstructure. Subject both groups to identical sliding wear tests at room temperature, intermediate, and high temperatures up to 800 °C. Compare the friction coefficients and wear rates as well as perform microstructural analyses before and after testing.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (via TEM/SEM) to verify the formation of nanoprecipitates and the in-situ glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated alloy does not show statistically significant reductions in both friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the control across the tested temperature range, or if the expected in-situ formed nanocrystalline glaze layer is not observed post-testing, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear.
